articles.description: It is Veterans Day again, which means that, alongside the free red, white, and blue pancake specials and complimentary coffees, Americans will post tributes honoring the ultimate sacrifice of our soldiers. Just as predictably, on Memorial Day, veterans will receive well-intentioned messages thanking them for their service. Of course, Memorial Day honors those who died while serving in the U.S. military, whereas Veterans Day recognizes all who have served. This confusion is hardly something to get worked up about in itself. But it is symptomatic of something more consequential: a nation detached from its military and the wars it fights. In a sense, Americans are not wrong to conflate the two holidays. articles.description: Last week, the Trump administration announced that, beginning January 1, South Africa and Rwanda will stop receiving preferential trade access to the U.S. market through the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA). But American interests themselves will suffer, as consumers will be forced to pay higher prices for the same goods. Despite their ideological disagreements, the two leaders held a cordial first summit that in subsequent months led to a resolution of their trade frictions, a $150 billion investment in shipbuilding, substantial investment in commercial projects in the United States, and even a surprise announcement that Trump would help Seoul build nuclear-powered submarines. One of Lee’s key commitments was to increase South Korean defense spending to 3.5% of GDP — the Trump administration’s minimum target for Asian nations. But what a difference a year can make with Trump. On October 21, U.S. Ambassador to South Korea Michelle Steel publicly described the relationship as experiencing “turbulence.” Lee’s government, for its part, has tried to downplay recent tensions, arguing that overheated domestic politics in both countries need not undermine the strong foundation of the alliance. articles.title: NYT the latest in showcasing bad US-China takes from DC experts
articles.description: A New York Times essay by former Biden administration officials Mira Rapp-Hooper and Ely Ratner published on Nov. 16, “Trump’s China Gamble Is Backfiring,” offers yet another in a long line of depressingly similar and one-sided arguments about China and U.S. China policy appearing across America’s major newspapers and foreign policy journals. The narrative goes like this, invariably: Beijing is ever more threatening in dire ways; Washington is responding inadequately; and only steadily increasing seemingly unlimited levels of American (and, in some examples, allied) military power and counter-pressure will restore stability and protect the West. Largely missing is a serious examination of how American and Chinese policies interact in creating perceived threats, and how credible reassurances, alongside deterrence, might reduce the danger and create lasting peace and prosperity. This outlook began to emerge to prominence with Washington’s embrace of strategic competition as the framework for U.S. China policy in late 2017 . articles.title: The biggest takeaway from trilateral is the nuclear piece
articles.description: The first trilateral meeting of Presidents Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin, held on November 19 in Shenzhen, was worth holding for one reason above all. The United States has a clear interest in reducing nuclear risks with both China and Russia, and the three leaders agreed to discuss how to do so . Beyond that, the summit yielded little for Washington. Xi gained the prestige of convening the three powers, while Putin gained stature on the world stage even as Russia continues its brutal war against Ukraine. The nuclear pledge deserves attention, however. Beijing has long resisted three-way arms-control negotiations, arguing that the United States and Russia should first reduce their much larger arsenals. China has discussed nuclear risks with both countries in the broader five-power process and held bilateral arms-control consultations with Washington in 2023. Beijing suspended further consultations in 2024, citing U.S. arms sales to Taiwan. What Shenzhen adds is Xi’s public commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and nonproliferation in a dedicated three-way format. articles.description: Not All Bond Carry Is Created Equal Authored by Eva Sun-Wai via M&G Investments' Bond Vigilantes , The word 'carry' is frequently thrown around in fixed income, and you will have heard many uses of it this year in the fashion of 'carry is back' or 'fixed income finally offers income again.' It is a crucial part of an underlying bond's return profile, and it is absolutely 'back,' but the purpose of this blog is to distinguish the important difference between having carry and being protected by carry. Today's starting yields offer an attractive entry point, but if the underlying bond is sufficiently volatile, a relatively modest yield move can erase a year's income quickly . When you factor in carry alongside rolldown and adjust for volatility, however, the 'carry cushion' can look pretty compelling. articles.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: this season’s big idea? Wear a skirt. It’s that simple
articles.description: All you need to look on-trend this autumn is a skirt, but instead of going shopping, check what you already have in your wardrobe I go to a lot of fashion shows, and sometimes they are gorgeous and sometimes they are ugly. Sometimes they are electrifying and sometimes they are deathly dull. Sometimes they are completely baffling. My absolute favourite kind of show is the one that makes me want to run home and change my outfit. A show that makes me think: there it is! That’s exactly what I want to wear. When the look speaks to me, as if it had been on the tip of my tongue. God, I love that. Which is what happened at Prada this season . The idea was: skirts. That’s it, that’s the whole idea. The show was 63 different skirts – some with a sweater, some with a bra top, some with a jacket, but the point was the skirts. They were knee-length, give or take an inch up or down, and A-line, although sometimes a narrow almost-pencil and other times with a broader flare. There were skirts that wrapped like kilts, held together with strips of industrial-weight Velcro embroidered with tiny gems. articles.title: I’m really hurt that my parents didn’t give me a 40th birthday gift | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
articles.description: You feel overlooked, but your parents’ disappointing behaviour does not necessarily mean they don’t love you I turned 40 a few years ago . For my 21st and 30th birthdays I got jewellery from my parents, so when they didn’t ask what I wanted, I assumed they would follow this tradition. But I got nothing. Not even an apology. It later transpired that they thought I was turning 41. But even then to receive nothing is hurtful . They blamed it on old age and said they had been struggling with their health. I place a lot of importance on gift giving . It isn’t about the value, but it’s nice to feel someone has spent time thinking about you . To get nothing just screamed that they didn’t care. articles.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.description: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). articles.title: Gout is on the rise – and excruciating. Why are sufferers still judged for it?
articles.description: About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma? Brett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout. “I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?” Continue reading...

articles.title: My search for Bologna’s perfect tagliatelle al ragù - the real ‘spag bol’
articles.description: The signature dish of Italy’s gastronomic capital is taken far more seriously than its British derivative. So which restaurant does the best ‘tag rag’? I used to eat spag bol three times a week. I’d have it every Friday at my nan’s, every Saturday at my dad’s, and every Tuesday at my mum’s. My nan would lean heavily on Dolmio and add a cheeky splash of Tabasco. My mum would rustle up hers in the time it took the pasta to cook, which gave it a crunchiness that sometimes made me cry (I swear to God, those onions were practically raw). And my dad would let his bubble away for the duration of Gladiators, meaning that by the time it was dished up at the start of Blind Date, it had an intensity that felt positively foreign. I’m not alone in being a big fan of spag bol – the dish is often voted the nation’s favourite, and there’s now even a National Spaghetti Bolognese Day (22 May) – but I do sometimes wonder what it is about this relatively simple import, essentially a combo of mince and tomatoes plonked upon pasta, that has won over millions and withstood the vagaries of time. So I travelled to the dish’s motherland, Bologna, to unlock its secrets and hunt down some prime examples. Cont

articles.title: Share your thoughts on Andy Burnham’s plan for a new EU deal
articles.description: We would like to hear your thoughts on the reopening of the Brexit debate Andy Burnham has announced that he will sign a new deal with the EU , arguing the UK has “lost more than we gained” since Brexit. “This is a win-win,” Burnham is expected to say at the lord mayor’s banquet in London on Monday, ahead of a summit with European leaders to secure agreements he says could raise GDP by £17bn. Continue reading...

articles.title: Is this Britain’s most beautiful bus journey? The Welsh service that beats the train hands down
articles.description: A new coach service between Holyhead in the north and Carmarthen in the south offers a thrilling glimpse of west Wales, from mountain peaks to pretty seafronts – and it knocks half an hour off the journey As anyone who has ever tried to catch a train from north to south Wales will know, it’s quite the adventure, and by adventure, I mean chore. You leave Wales, dip into England and then back into Wales to complete the journey. The fastest “Marches” route, which includes stops in Chester, Crewe and Shrewsbury, takes about five and a half hours and costs about £105, depending on your ticket. There are lots of reasons for this: mid-Wales has some challenging topography; the old rail networks, before the Beeching cuts, predominantly bled outwards, transporting slate, coal and steel to distant ports and markets. Last month, all that changed. Just not in the way you probably imagine. Continue reading...

articles.title: India has been named a ‘destination of the year’ for 2027 – here are insiders’ tips on travelling beyond the tropes
articles.description: As tourism booms, three experienced female travellers give their take on how to make the most of travelling here • Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge. India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities. Continue reading...

articles.title: Don’t buy new tech this Black Friday: expert tips for buying refurbished phones and laptops
articles.description: Tech on its last legs? Refurbished can be the cheaper, greener option. Here’s how to choose well and avoid the pitfalls • How to make your phone last longer • The best sustainable Black Friday deals Even if you do your best to avoid it, it’s hard to escape the noise of retailers offering implausible-seeming Black Friday discounts on desirable technology. What they won’t be so keen to highlight is the huge environmental cost that comes from feeding the capitalist beast year on year, given what an obvious sales vibe-killer it would be. While the best approach for the planet is to opt out completely and observe the alternative holiday of Buy Nothing Day instead, such an approach can prove self-defeating for your finances in the long term. If you shop smart on Black Friday and avoid the lure of impulse buys, it’s a good time to stock up on the things you need at lower prices than the rest of the year. Continue reading...

articles.title: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience
articles.description: PC; Forward Instinct This irreverent stealth game depicts Samuel’s lonely life robbing garish, midwestern abodes – it’s a Shameless way to make a living For many people, McMansions are an eyesore, but for the protagonist of Keepsake County, a renowned burglar, they are an enticing opportunity. Prowling at purple-hued dusk, this unfussy thief is just as likely to steal a half-eaten slice of pizza or a naff ceramic ornament as he is an expensive set of golf clubs. It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag. Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. Rather, it is a stealing simulator with eccentric Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurdist sense of humour that is expressed in its moment-to-moment action. For example, when I set off the alarm at a glinting modernist abode, I had to quickly dodge the gunshot fired my way by its maniacal owner, and as I scarpered across the surrounding grassy verge, I grabbed und

articles.title: After Eight: the story of Satpal Ram - documentary
articles.description: It is 40 years since a racially charged attack at a curry house led to Satpal Ram’s conviction for murder, but today Britain’s post-pub curry culture still has a dark side. Ram spent 24 years in prison before a global campaign for justice, led by bands including Asian Dub Foundation and Primal Scream, secured his release from prison. His case raises crucial questions about the UK’s ongoing struggle for racial equality Continue reading...

articles.title: Get vaccinated, don’t vape – and moisturise liberally! 10 doctors on how to avoid and treat winter ailments
articles.description: The nights are drawing in, the temperature is dropping, festive overindulgence is on the horizon and it’s easy to get run down. Here’s some expert advice to help you safely through the season Winter can be a challenging time, with bad weather, dark evenings, horrible bugs circulating, plus plenty of opportunities for overindulging. How can we avoid getting run down? Doctors share their tips for surviving the season, from saunas to screen blockers, light boxes to apples. Continue reading...

articles.title: Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to rise by 26% to £2,166 from January
articles.description: Government under pressure to help households as increase would add £443 to average annual dual-fuel bill Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers Tell us: are you shopping around for a better deal? UK inflation rises to 3.6% Energy bills across Great Britain are predicted to reach £2,166 a year for the typical household from January as the impact of the Middle East conflict piles pressure on the government to offer more support to hard-hit households. The government’s cap on gas and electricity prices is likely to rise by 26% early next year, equivalent to adding £443 to the average annual dual-fuel bill, in one of the biggest quarterly price rises on record, according to the leading forecaster Cornwall Insight. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The sea washed away trees, then a whole row of houses. I knew it was time to get out’ – This is climate breakdown
articles.description: She noticed the trees going first. Slowly she understood that the sea was going to take the whole village. This is Guadalupe Cobos Pacheco’s story Location: El Bosque, Mexico Disaster: Sea encroachment The fishing village of El Bosque was the first community in Mexico to be recogni sed as climate-displaced. The inhabitants were moved in 2023 . By then, coastal erosion and flooding had already taken many of the homes. Continue reading...

articles.title: Nicola Coughlan on her favourite noodles, getting rejected from drama school and I Am Helen
articles.description: What does Lady Whistledown eat when nobody's watching?  This week on Comfort Eating, Siobhán McSweeney is joined by the brilliant Nicola Coughlan, star of Derry Girls and Bridgerton, for a seriously fun catch-up involving comfort food, childhood nostalgia and some VERY questionable food combinations. Nicola brings her ultimate comfort food to the table: think fusion - or perhaps it’s confusion. There's also Diet Coke mixed with pickle juice (yes, really), stories about growing up in Galway, and her Supermac's Gold Card. Plus, Nicola reflects on her journey into acting, drama school rejection, the early struggles of making it in London and how life changed after Derry Girls and Bridgerton. Continue reading...

articles.title: Gjak by Dimosthenis Papamarkos review – sensational tales of wartime Greek struggle
articles.description: Translated into English in thrilling style, these interlinked stories of ambushes and vendettas vividly evoke the bitter conflict of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war Nine interconnected tales about the violence of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war, and the struggles of its broken soldiers to reassimilate into civilian life, Gjak is something of a sensation. Originally written in Greek and Arvanitic, a dialect spoken by a Greco-Albanian ethnic group, and featuring characters from an unspecified Arvanite village, it was a hit in Greece in 2014 and comes to the UK in an agile translation by Siân Valvis. In her fascinating introductory note, Valvis writes of her attempt to capture the “unruly, galloping force” of Dimosthenis Papamarkos’s prose. She succeeds in thrilling style. Delivered in a demotic, gossipy voice, these are rough-hewn stories of ambushes and vendettas, of brothers in arms being “closer than kin” and of lingering, sour regret. One of the translations of the eponymous Arvanitic word “ gjak ” is “blood” and indeed, graphic bloodiness is inescapable. Narrators don’t shy away from descriptions of how “shrapnel sliced [them] up like a fillet – eyes, teeth, ripped off half a jaw”.

articles.title: The Man Who Broke Reality by Philip Ball review – the inspirational genius of Niels Bohr
articles.description: Scientific discoveries are explained effortlessly in this portrait of a man whose research was driven by pure passion Niels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work. But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Today he would probably be considered neurodivergent; he possessed a passion for physics that cast a spell on all who knew him. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood. Continue reading...

articles.title: A moment that changed me: the tomato pasta that became an obsession – and helped me lead a better life
articles.description: At a restaurant in Italy in 2022, every forkful of my meal made my eyes close and mouth water. For four years since, I have tried to recreate this dish. The pursuit has finally made me a proper vegetarian I’ve ostensibly been vegetarian for 13 years and, in that time, I’ve eaten a lot of meat. My mum used to leave out the last bit of lamb madras, with a wink, then loudly announce that she was going to bed. I have accidentally found myself in KFC at midnight, hood up, drunk, looking both ways and asking for a Bargain Bucket. My partner once came home early from a night out and caught me red-handed, in bed with McDonald’s Chicken Selects. Such incidents were infrequent moments of weakness and, after the fact, I was always racked with guilt. But for most of my vegetarian life, I had felt a certain emptiness; a gaping meat-shaped hole in my heart and stomach. Then I ate a bowl of pasta. It was 2022 and an Italian university friend, Mattia, invited me to Tuscany. I spent four days with his lovely family, in the rolling verdant hills, with fireflies and fallow deer keeping us company, drinking vernaccia and talking of books and art and poetry. But none of that matters, not even a bit. Al

articles.title: Life insurance: what is it and do you need it?
articles.description: It could protect you and your family in the event of death or accident – and in some cases it costs no more than a TV streaming service No one wants to spend time imagining the worst thing that could happen, and perhaps that is why about 60% of UK adults have no life insurance, or why more people have pet insurance than have income protection for if they become too sick to work. However, there are certain milestones in life, such as having children or taking on a mortgage, that focus the mind on what might happen if things do go wrong. How would your family manage if you or your partner died? How would you cover the mortgage if you had an accident and couldn’t work? Continue reading...

articles.title: Pill that mimics Viagra can slow Alzheimer’s progression, study suggests
articles.description: Experts call trial results of medication that slowed cognitive decline by almost a third ‘very promising’ A pill that mimics Viagra by relaxing blood vessels and increasing blood flow to the brain can slow cognitive decline in people with Alzheimer’s disease by almost a third, a global study suggests. Alzheimer’s is the most common form of dementia, a condition that is forecast to affect 153 million people worldwide by 2050. There is currently no cure. Continue reading...

articles.title: I jumped from a plane at 12,000ft. In mid-air, a friend’s knee collided into my neck
articles.description: A group of eight trainee parachutists did the jump, and not far from the ground, disaster struck. Rob Bugden describes how he rebuilt his life after the accident that changed everything The skydive was going to plan. At 12,000ft, Rob Bugden jumped from the plane, quickly getting himself stable by arching his back to create a solid base. He checked for speed and altitude on his watch, and when he was low enough, pulled the parachute’s toggles. “I looked up. Good canopy.” But then: “Cut to black. And I’m waking up in a hospital in Phoenix.” It was 21 January 2016, the final day of his Royal Air Force high altitude training in the US, when 30-year-old Bugden collided – mid-air – with his friend, Brook Stebbings. They were moving into the landing stack formation, a vertical queue of eight parachutists flying in a holding pattern at different altitudes, when, at approximately 1,000ft, Stebbings’ knee crashed into him, breaking his neck. They fell to the sand in the middle of the desert, entangled – looking, according to the team on the ground, “like we had a bag of washing above our heads”. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I hope paramedics are on standby for the sex scenes!’ The wet and wild TV experience leaving fans dizzy
articles.description: From icy squirts to bed-bouncing vibrations, erotic hockey drama Heated Rivalry just got even raunchier in ‘extreme sensory’ 4DX cinema screenings. But one scene proved too much – even for the super fans I’m in the cinema foyer when I first spot them: hockey jerseys. Lots of them. “I’ve no idea what to expect!” giggles Chloe, who is wearing a black and yellow “Rozanov” jersey. Like me, she has never been to a 4DX screening before – but when Cineworld announced it would be showing episodes five and six of queer hockey drama Heated Rivalry in the novel format, she booked tickets immediately. “I actually had tickets for the 2D screening, but cancelled them for this,” she says. Over the last two weeks, Heated Rivalry fans have been treated to big screen marathons of Jacob Tierney’s hit TV show, based on Rachel Reid’s bestselling book series, Game Changers. But 4DX is next level. The “extreme sensory” cinema technology is usually deployed for high-octane action flicks – films with epic battles or chase sequences. Still, with Cineworld offering the opportunity to “immerse yourself in the motion, wind, water [and] scent” of major league hockey’s raunchiest fictional romance, who could res

articles.title: ‘Cherubino’s in’t’ cupboard’: Mozart via Bradford and Bollywood is a blast
articles.description: Bradford Arts Centre Ian McMillan’s south Yorkshire language version of The Marriage of Figaro sets the opera in 1970s Bradford. Indian classical instruments join to the reworked score in this high-energy, low-budget and hugely enjoyable take ‘This will be better than Barnsley FC,” I overheard the poet, broadcaster and professional Yorkshireman Ian McMillan assuring a friend ahead of curtain-up on his dialect adaptation of Mozart’s The Marriage of Figaro. “Everything’s better than Barnsley FC.” I don’t know much about League One football, I admit, but this high-energy, low-budget production directed by Alex Chisholm for Bradford Opera Festival punches far above its weight and could definitely survive less self-deprecating comparisons. Continue reading...

articles.title: Twenty years ago, the Wii and PS3 predicted the future of gaming – did they get it right?
articles.description: Both launched in 2006, with contrasting visions of gaming – one focused on accessibility, the other on technical ambition – each leaving a lasting legacy • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The main focus of the games industry this week is, of course, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI – a game that could define the next decade for the industry. For this week’s newsletter though, I wanted to direct your attention two decades into the past. In November 2006, two console manufacturers launched their competing – and wildly different – visions of what the future of video games would look like. Twenty years later, it’s clear that somehow they were both right. And yet, in some ways, they were both wrong. For Nintendo, the Wii was the natural extension of its famous maxim, Kareta Gijutsu no Suihei Shikō – roughly translated as lateral thinking with withered technology. Coined by the company’s legendary engineer Gunpei Yokoi, father of the Game Boy, the phrase described a philosophy in which old tech could be combined with smart ideas to provide amazing new gaming possibilities. The Game Boy itself used a slow, old Sharp LR35902 processor and a sickly green mo

articles.title: The best TVs in the UK for every home and screen size, tested
articles.description: Not sure which TV is right for you? Whether you want an affordable mini LED or a feature-packed OLED, here’s what our square-eyed expert recommends • Do you really need to buy a new TV? How to upgrade your setup If your TV looks like an off-cut from Stonehenge, isn’t quite as smart as your microwave or, heaven forfend, is boring old HD rather than 4K HDR (high dynamic range), it could be time to invest in something more up to date. But even a cursory look at the latest TVs available will confirm a bewildering array of options, from super-slim models with unfeasibly large screens to high performers that rival the picture quality at your local cinema. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Opposites don’t attract’: Adam Grant on how to strengthen friendships and make new ones faster
articles.description: The organisational psychologist and bestselling author says learning about the four types of platonic bonds can help us understand our relationships Here’s a stat to ruin your day: of all the people you would call a friend, research suggests only about half would reciprocate. The thought might make you want to wipe your contacts list and start afresh. But let’s look on the positive side, suggests Adam Grant, the Wharton organisational psychologist and New York Times bestselling author of Originals, and Hidden Potential. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Deeply concerning’: NHS in England reports more than 3,000 incidents of staff snooping on patients’ records
articles.description: Campaign groups and regulators say data breaches are distressing for patients and families and erode trust in the health service The NHS in England has recorded more than 3,000 incidents of staff inappropriately snooping on patients’ medical records in the last five years. Patient campaign groups and regulators said the figures were “deeply concerning” and distressing for patients and families, and eroded trust in the health service. A lack of transparency from NHS organisations after data breaches were uncovered further compounded the heartache, they added. Continue reading...

articles.title: Dashing through the snow: 10 of the UK’s best Christmas train rides
articles.description: Heritage railways will soon be steaming into action, with special departures offering winter landscapes, seasonal goodies and a chance to meet Father Christmas Red tablecloths, festive decor and tartan upholstered carriage seats bring the yuletide vibe onboard Strathspey Railway’s Elf Express. From your first-class carriage of either a steam-hauled or heritage diesel engine, you will be served sandwiches and cakes from traditional tiered plates, washed down with hot drinks and fizz. Santa and his elves will visit your carriage with presents for children, otherwise sit back and enjoy the woodland and moorland scenery of rural Speyside on this 20-mile round-trip (lasting about 1 hour and 40 minutes) between Aviemore and Broomhill. Weekends and select weekdays until 24 December, £260 for four people . Continue reading...

articles.title: UK businesses: what are the barriers stopping you hiring young people?
articles.description: We want to hear from people who own or run companies in Britain who are trying to hire under-25s. What obstacles do you face? Labour’s long-awaited review into youth joblessness published this week recommended that ministers cut business taxes and ease regulations to encourage employers to hire more young people. Alan Milburn’s report into how to address the nearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training in the UK also proposes setting up a youth opportunity service to provide support and advice to give every young person a guaranteed route into education, training or work. Continue reading...

articles.title: UK energy bills are rising. Tell us: are you shopping around for a better deal?
articles.description: We’d like to hear from UK households about whether they’re switching energy suppliers to save money or finding that deals are too similar to make it worthwhile Energy bills in Great Britain are forecast to rise by 26% from January, adding £443 to the typical household’s annual bill. The increase, driven by rising gas prices amid the Middle East conflict, would be one of the biggest quarterly rises on record, according to forecaster Cornwall Insight. Are you shopping around for a better gas or electricity deal or have you decided to stay with your current supplier? What has influenced your decision? Continue reading...

articles.title: Guarding Stars review – Leighton Meester is a delight in fizzy Netflix holiday romance
articles.description: As a female bodyguard protecting an A-list star, the Gossip Girl actor shines in Christmas movie a cut above the competition Though it is my personal opinion that Christmas should not begin until after Thanksgiving, I am pleased to say that we already have at least one treat in Netflix’s holiday movie assembly line: Guarding Stars, starring Leighton Meester as a frosty bodyguard tasked with protecting Jared Padalecki’s movie star at, of all places, his family’s Montana ranch, falls on the fizzy side of seasonal fluff. Good holiday movies are an exercise in knowing silliness, and so it is a relief when the first 10 minutes of this movie, directed by Elizabeth Allen Rosenbaum, strikes the rare December balance between hearth-like warmth (the twinkle in Meester’s chocolate eyes when her Hannah Brooks lands a verbal punch) and complete lunacy (she lands that punch in an argument with her ex about … cuddling … literally seconds after thwarting an assassination attempt in Times Square). As a homespun band of hot would-be cowboys later drawl at a Christmas parade in “Montana” (Canada, per usual): “Christmas is back, y’all.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Bloomscrolling: the uplifting new way to waste your own time
articles.description: Tired of your social media feeds being a bin fire? Want more beauty? Gen Z are training their algorithms – and it’s working wonders for them Name: Bloomscrolling. Age: The term has been floating around for a few years, but it has recently taken off on TikTok. Continue reading...

articles.title: You Can See Everything review – unblinking, unhinged and unmissable
articles.description: Nathan Fielder’s intense close-range study of fraudster Elizabeth Holmes is as gripping as any thriller • This review contains spoilers Thrillingly reckless, deliciously irresponsible and as gripping as any thriller, this situationist docu-hybrid masterpiece from co-directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim gets up close and personal with convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes . It was Holmes’s US biotech firm Theranos, run jointly with her then partner Sunny Balwani, which in 2003 notoriously claimed to have invented a little box that could diagnose all manner of illnesses from a single drop of blood, its corporate prestige pumped by credulous board members including George Schultz and Henry Kissinger. Yet Holmes has now met her match, perhaps even her predatory-platonic love match, in the film’s presenter Nathan Fielder, who is basically the Aleister Crowley of modern documentary satire, the hilarious dark master of turning truth into fiction and back again. His film delivers an extraordinary twist at around the halfway mark, and readers wanting to preserve the shock had better bail out here. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I came close to killing Sally about six times’: how my abusive father was enabled by his fame
articles.description: Like Russell Brand, my father was put on a pedestal by the media, despite a history of troubling, misogynistic comments. Meanwhile, my mother suffered through years of appalling treatment Even though decades have passed, part of me feels I should not be telling this story. Not because it isn’t true, but because telling makes it real. And the reality is very hard to bear. I was a young child at home in Whitechapel, east London, when my mother came into my bedroom, which was next to my parents’, and told me that my father had raped her. He had gone off to work and I was too young to fully understand what the words meant – perhaps seven or eight – and I remember being angry with her for upsetting life again, as she had done before, when she suddenly came to me at the top of the stairs and told me that they would “have to part” and that would mean taking me away with her. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Altruists review – two of TV’s best actors light up this chaotic crypto tale
articles.description: Julia Garner and Anthony Boyle play the FTX founders behind ‘the greatest fraud ever committed’ in the US. It’s a mind-boggling story – just make sure you don’t miss a single moment What happens when you put really stupid clever people in charge of the world? Not as presidents (they currently trend mostly towards the merely stupid) or prime ministers (generally neither really stupid nor really clever), but in charge of the real world, which is to say the online world, the one that really governs us? We are watching that play out day by day, but if you have enough slack left in your dread-system, a cortisol spike yet to execute, why not add a warning from history to your consumption of horrors? Welcome to The Altruists, a breakneck breakdown of the brief career of Sam Bankman-Fried (played by Anthony Boyle) who, with his on-off girlfriend Caroline Ellison (played by Julia Garner), set up the cryptocurrency exchange FTX with the belief that it would revolutionise finance and – as the increasingly absurd/dishonest/knowingly satirical Silicon Valley mantra has it – make the world a better place. A very few years later, FTX – worth $36bn (£27bn) at its peak – collapsed and in 2023 the p

articles.title: Nothing but highlights: is Power Slap the sport we deserve?
articles.description: Slap fighting is the world’s newest combat sport. Built for short attention spans and super-viral moments, it’s aiming for global dominance. No flinching In the days before Power Slap 22, in Belgrade, Serbia, in late July, the organisers of the world’s newest combat sport were taking no chances. At the Crowne Plaza hotel, where competitors were booked to stay, those facing off had been separated by floor, lest any unauthorised violence took place. It turned out there was little need. The night before the main event, contestants mingled amiably in the lobby and bar. The atmosphere was more specialist sales conference than brewing barroom brawl. In the lobby, I joined Louis “Razor” Robinson, and Ryan “the Punisher” Kenny. “We’re all friends in slap,” Robinson said, earnestly, by way of a greeting. Robinson, a Brit from Stalybridge, Greater Manchester, is 30, stout, intense. Kenny, a Canadian, is 34, lofty, laid back. Continue reading...

articles.title: Want to shop more sustainably this Black Friday? The best UK deals on eco-friendly products we love
articles.description: Save money and help the planet with these genuine discounts on everything from bamboo toilet paper to B Corp-certified bedding • Expert tips for buying refurbished phones and laptops • The best early Black Friday deals Ethical and sustainable probably aren’t the first words that spring to mind when you think of Black Friday. The annual price-slashing jamboree sits cunningly in wait for your final payday before Christmas, hoping that the dangled carrot of a few quid off will make you more likely to overconsume and overspend. Approach it with care, though, and Black Friday is a good opportunity to buy eco-friendly products that might normally stretch your budget. Many of our Filter recommendations tick either the green box or the affordable box, but we (and you, I expect) would be a lot happier if more of them ticked both. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tories select James Cleverly as candidate for London mayor
articles.description: Former home secretary wins 86% support in a membership vote to stand in May 2028 James Cleverly has been chosen by the Conservatives as their candidate in the next London mayoral election, with the former cabinet minister saying he would stand up to “anti-London” Andy Burnham. Cleverly, who stood down as shadow communities secretary in August to focus on his mayoral ambitions, was overwhelmingly chosen in a vote of London Tory members from a three-strong shortlist, winning 86% of the ballot. Continue reading...

articles.title: Eight injured after driver in Israel repeatedly rams car into Palestinians
articles.description: Arab MPs accuse politicians of fuelling hostility as footage shows driver accelerating towards Palestinians at four locations in Kafr Qasim Eight people were injured on Wednesday evening when a driver struck Palestinian residents at four separate locations in Kafr Qasim, a city in central Israel. Footage shared on social media appears to show the car accelerating towards people, all Palestinians, at several locations in the city, striking them before driving away. Three of those injured were in moderate condition, and several of the victims were women leaving a nearby wedding, the Times of Israel reported . Continue reading...

articles.title: Robert Pattinson to apply for 90,000 more jobs? UK government trolls James Bond actor
articles.description: Westminster joins wave of ‘job-stealing’ memes after the actor’s late success edging out the other contenders to be the new 007 Everybody is trying to get a piece of the Bond action: even the UK government. In a post on its official Instagram account , the UK government promoted its youth jobs guarantee scheme, first announced in August , with a picture of Robert Pattinson as Bond with the joke caption: “Robert Pattinson to apply for all 90,000 jobs created for young people through Youth Employment Scheme.” Continue reading...

articles.title: IPCC report delay will threaten global effort to tackle climate crisis, says top scientist
articles.description: Johan Rockström, one of world’s leading climate experts, says slowing down scientific work puts cooperation at risk Climate science is “foundational” to the Paris agreement and worldwide progress on tackling global heating, and attempts to delay new scientific reports threaten global cooperation on tackling the crisis, one of the world’s leading climate scientists has warned. Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, must be allowed to work as quickly as possible on its next comprehensive assessment of global knowledge of the climate systems . Continue reading...

articles.title: Trance, prog synths, guttural screaming: Lorenzo Senni’s All Ages is the year’s wildest electronic album
articles.description: (Warp) The Milan producer revisits his youth as a straight-edge punk fan voyeuristically dabbling in rave – and finds a thrilling interzone between both genres The opening line of the biography on Lorenzo Senni’s Bandcamp page is striking. “Lorenzo Senni was never a raver,” it reads, something of a blunt admission from a dance producer, or at least a producer who works in an area of electronica influenced by dance music: one might reasonably assume you need some first-hand experience of the dancefloor’s ineffable freedom in order to make music for it. But the Milan-based Senni has made a USP out of his arm’s length distance from what that Bandcamp bio calls a “neon-hued chemical world”. A straight-edge punk fan in the late 90s, he accompanied friends to Rimini’s hardcore and gabber clubs as a kind of anthropological exercise, a self-styled “rave voyeur” who “just liked to observe and analyse my surroundings”. Accordingly, his albums to date have dealt in what approving critics like to call deconstructions or interrogations of dance music rather than dance music itself: 2012’s Quantum Jelly and 2014’s Superimpositions featured what Senni called “pointillistic trance”, spinning the i

articles.title: You be the judge: should my friend stop eating smelly meals at work?

articles.title: This year, the Greens have reshaped British politics. Now we need party systems to match that influence | Caroline Lucas
articles.description: Without Zack Polanski and Hannah Spencer, we might still be stuck with Keir Starmer. But after some difficult weeks, our party needs an overhaul Caroline Lucas is co-chair of the cross-party campaign group Compass and a former Green MP In the aftermath of some difficult weeks for the Greens, one encouraging response has particularly stood out for me: the widespread agreement across progressive politics that the UK is better for having a strong Green party. One that will hold other parties to account for their delivery on social and environmental justice and that will put issues on the political agenda that other parties won’t. From Rosebank to wealth taxes and ending arms sales to Israel, Greens are stretching the Overton window so that the gap narrows between what’s necessary and what’s currently deemed politically acceptable. As we increasingly win more council seats, assembly members, mayors and MPs, we are able, at all levels of government, to help restore the natural world, tackle climate breakdown and challenge the economic framework of neoliberalism that has governed us for too long. articles.title: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras
articles.description: We can’t make AI safe for humanity if tech bosses are allowed to run their companies like autocracies Over the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI’s product releases said he was quitting the ChatGPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. As a society we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle – and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal: as the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice. Isabelle Ferreras is accelerator fellow at the University of Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI, FNRS research director at the University of Louvain, Belgium and co-founder of Dem

The paintings are square, because a square is neutral, and he didn’t want viewers associating them with the visual language of landscape or portrait. For Ryman, his paintings resolutely were what they were, which is to say, white paint applied to various surfaces and fixed to the wall. Not “windows” through which one could glimpse another world. At the National Gallery, a couple of miles across town, is an exhibition of 10 works by the 15th-century Flemish painter Jan van Eyck. With one exception – the Arnolfini portrait, which is a one-off in all kinds of ways – they are all A4-size portraits, each angled so that we see more of the left than the right side of their faces. articles.description: This unusual portrait of a young girl whose prison visits are interweaved with her grandmother’s war-weary reminiscences rewards attention American author Harriet Clark’s first novel, partly inspired by her own life, is narrated by a girl whose mother is in prison. Suzanna is being raised by grandparents while her mother serves a life sentence for driving the getaway car for a botched bank robbery intended to fund revolutionary political activism. Although Suzanna refuses the narrative, in some ways this is a coming-of-age story, but with a protagonist whose overwhelming need is to go nowhere and change nothing. The Hill is shaped by the tension between the novel’s need for a plot and Suzanna’s rejection of her own role in the Bildungsroman. Prison visits structure Suzanna’s life, their rituals and repetitions at once marking and resisting the passage of time. At first, her grandfather drives her from their shabby urban apartment to the hilltop prison and escorts her to the entrance to the children’s centre, where on a good day the prisoners are allowed to play with their children under close surveillance. Later, the grandfather dies, activities in the centre are restricted and Suz

articles.title: ‘Perhaps we are safer not knowing’: a year after his death, Rob Reiner’s JFK assassination book is revealed
articles.description: The late director worked with David Hoffman and Dick Russell on a book about his lifelong fascination with what really happened on 22 November 1963 On 8 December last year, the great director Rob Reiner signed off the prologue for Who Killed JFK? , his book written with David Hoffman and Dick Russell and based on his podcast with Soledad O’Brien. Describing a lifelong fascination with the assassination of John F Kennedy in Dallas on 22 November 1963, and what he saw as the vast conspiracy to cover up who really killed the 35th president, Reiner wrote: “Maybe, people don’t truly want an answer. Perhaps we are safer not knowing … Well, I’m done being safe.” Six days later, Reiner and his wife, Michelle Reiner, were stabbed to death in their home. As Owain Glyndŵr, beacon of Welsh resistance, he doesn’t disappoint. “We can die gently and be forgotten,” he exhorts his followers. “Or we can rage .” Rage and resignation, the sword and the song, resonate through Gary Owen’s absorbing medieval epic for Wales Millennium Centre and Sheen’s new Welsh National Theatre . articles.title: The Thanksgiving food traditions we could all share
articles.description: Warming pie, buttery mash and plenty of gravy are a perfect excuse to gather friends around the table during chilly November • Sign up here for our weekly food newsletter, Feast As a Brit, there are plenty of reasons for me not to embrace Thanksgiving, most of all because it isn’t actually a British holiday, and least of all because we already have quite enough occasions to eat ourselves silly between now and January. And yet, every November, as the days grow shorter and darker and colder, I find myself rather taken with the idea of hosting a seasonal dinner for friends. If Christmas is more formal and family-focused, then Thanksgiving feels like a prime opportunity to get pals around the table, eat until you need to undo your top trouser button, and take a moment to appreciate what you have. And if that means borrowing a few ideas from across the Atlantic – a warming spiced pumpkin pie , say, or a dish of fruity stuffing and a sharp cranberry sauce – well, there’s no reason we can’t make them our own. Obviously there are some crossovers with Britain’s main festive meal, turkey being the big one. Personally, I prefer to cook a cockerel on Christmas Day, which naturally gives me the

articles.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for pasta all’arrabbiata with red onion and plums | A kitchen in Rome
articles.description: Much like tomato, the plum has a natural acidity and sweetness that works brilliantly in a delightfully jammy pasta sauce Standing on platform 2 at Baker Street station a few weeks ago, a grey creature scuttled under the raised tracks. “You’re never more than six feet away from a rat in London,” I said to my Roman son. “It’s a mouse, Mum,” was his hardboiled reply to my rehashing of an urban myth. A myth that turns out to be inaccurate, according to Dr David Cowan , whose research on the subject resulted in estimates of anything from 10ft-164ft: in other words, while it’s impossible to know for sure, in certain areas you might be very close to a rat. The same can be said about wild plum trees all over the world. While it’s impossible to know exactly, even in dense urban areas, you might be very close to a wild plum tree or, more correctly, a cultivated plum that has gone feral. Hedgerows, field margins, woodland edges, abandoned parks and wastelands are all places in which you might find yourself close to a plum tree; its branches decorated with fruit, some the size of marbles, others lozenges or eggs, and their spectrum of colour ranging from deep purple to powdery light blue, red

articles.title: Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers
articles.description: It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the forecast rise next year Average energy bill in Great Britain predicted to rise to £2,166 The energy price cap in Great Britain looks likely to go up by 26% in January . But your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving. Providers are offering fixed tariffs that work out up to £407 below the estimated price cap, according to price comparison website uSwitch. It’s worth noting that it’s the price of the energy you use that is fixed, not your bill – so you will still be charged according to what you use. Continue reading...

Gig crews drag their boats up the slipway, away from the ebbing water. Lime-loving old man’s beard on riverside bushes reminds us of the cargoes of limestone, once shipped with coal to these quays for burning in the monumental kilns. Upriver, the woodland path towards the river cliff chapel is strewn with dry leaves, and beech and sweet chestnut hang on to green and golden foliage. The National Trust’s valley garden remains in shade, apart from the fiery top of a swamp cypress , brilliant against the blue sky. Continue reading...

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
articles.description: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? articles.description: David Fincher directs Quentin Tarantino’s script, picking up from Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, and its lead is more ineffably beguiling than ever We got through to the very end of Quentin Tarantino’s previous film Once Upon a Time in Hollywood without finding out exactly how, why or if Brad Pitt’s stuntman character Cliff Booth murdered his wife. It was an issue only addressed in Tarantino’s novel based on the movie. And throughout the 140 minutes of this outrageous sugar-rush sequel – scripted by Tarantino and directed by David Fincher – this subject is tactfully passed over in silence, the one point that damages our perception of Cliff’s amiable-cowpoke good nature. Cliff is the guy who climaxed the previous picture by helping with a dramatic rescue; after, that is, gallantly refusing an age-gap relationship with Margaret Qualley’s jailbait teen. Well, we may not get the complete picture of Cliff’s matrimonial circumstances until Tarantino’s forthcoming crossover Cliff Booth novel, with which this film is to form a kind of multimedia narrative event. articles.title: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel
articles.description: Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intent The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states. In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent. articles.title: How to start eating plant-based, without missing out on nutrients or foods you enjoy
articles.description: Experts agree that if you’re thinking of changing your diet, start small and keep your goals in mind At this point, the environmental effects of the meat industry have been well-established: one 2021 study found that meat accounts for nearly 60% of all greenhouse gases from food production, and a 2025 report estimated that animal agriculture was responsible for 12%-19% of total human-caused greenhouse gases. According to the United Nations, one of the best things people can do to reduce their personal carbon footprint is shift from a diet heavy in meat to one that is more plant-based. articles.title: The moral panic over Neets needs to stop. The problem is bad jobs, not young people | Aditya Chakrabortty
articles.description: Milburn’s review doesn’t ask what kind of work young people will be going into: zero hours, minimum wage, mind-numbing. Do we have the guts to solve that? One big number has been repeated over and over this week: 1 million. As ministers and journalists keep telling us, about 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds are not in education, employment or training (Neet). They’re the subject of Alan Milburn’s review, which, although not commissioned by Andy Burnham, has become the first big policy of his new government. Rather than launch into my conclusions, let me give you three more numbers by which to judge Milburn for yourself. These figures have not appeared in any of this week’s coverage, but to understand the review’s context and its chances of success they are vital. Aditya Chakrabortty is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.title: Anthropic keeps the AI party swinging, but the atmosphere is bubbly | Nils Pratley
articles.description: Can the newly listed AI company really be worth $2tn? Anyone who remembers the late 1990s has good reason to ask Business live – latest updates Roll up, roll up, who wants to buy shares in a company whose technology “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, as the prospectus had it? Virtually everybody, as it turned out. Anthropic flew out of the blocks on its first day as a listed company . From the point of view of the promoters, the result was as good as it gets. The final pricing for the shares at $83 apiece was meaningfully higher than the indicated range of $70 to $78, but still left room for a big initial “pop”. articles.title: It’s unfashionable to say it, but class still matters – and young people know that | Polly Toynbee
articles.description: From inheritance to nepotism in the workplace, social inequality is now a daily experience for many young people This should come as no great surprise: young people are more keenly aware of the significance of social class than those who came before them. The yawning gap in life chances at birth is something they know better than complacent older generations. Class may be unfashionable in the language of politics – long damned by the right as the politics of envy, avoided by many on the left for fear of sounding chip-on-the-shoulder – yet it’s part of the daily experience for young people. Nearly half of 16- to 34-year-olds in the UK now say class is important to their identity – and not in a good way – according to a new Ipsos poll . That’s nearly twice as many as among the over-55s. Maybe that’s because more young people are better educated at each level, so they know more, with a grounding in reasoned thinking. articles.title: Parents: please don’t buy Grand Theft Auto VI for your child
articles.description: Rockstar Games’ brilliant 18-rated criminal caper is stuffed with sex, drugs and violence. It is the most explicit game I’ve ever played – and it really is not for kids Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? I am haunted still by an interaction I had at my stepson’s ninth birthday party in 2014, where one of the kids asked if I could put on Grand Theft Auto V for them all. “I have it at home!”, he said, giving me the puppy-dog eyes. Mentally replaying that game in my head, flashing back to the many scenes involving such things as smoking meth, over-the-top gratuitous violence and grubby sex in one character’s trailer, I said “ no way” . Later I gently mentioned to the kid’s mother that GTA V was an 18-rated game and really wasn’t suitable for kids. “Oh, but he’s really good at these games,” she told me. She was genuinely shocked to learn that an 18-rating on a video game was a flag for adult content, rather than an indication of its difficulty. Grand Theft Auto VI is released this week. articles.title: The Guardian view on the international court of justice: the ruling against Myanmar should be only the start for the Rohingya | Editorial
articles.description: A landmark finding of genocide marked a good day for international law. But both the court and the Rohingya minority now need sustained support The finding of the world’s highest court that Myanmar committed genocide is a landmark in international law. But at the heart of this case are “real people, real stories and a real group of human beings”, as Dawda Jallow, the Gambian justice minister, stressed in bringing it. This was one test of how the world has responded to the persecution of the mostly Muslim Rohingya minority in Rakhine state. The international community’s response to the majority judgment will be another. This is the first time that the international court of justice (ICJ) has found a state guilty of genocide. Around 10,000 Rohingya were killed in the 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military, in many cases gunned down as they fled, with another 700,000 escaping to Bangladesh. The judges found that the aim was to destroy “a substantial part” of the Rohingya people, with the murder of infants, widespread sexual violence and razing of villages not accounted for simply by military objectives. articles.title: The Guardian view on Grand Theft Auto VI: a game that makes players think twice | Editorial
articles.description: For almost 30 years, Grand Theft Auto has revelled in America’s vices. Its latest instalment may find room for empathy amid the mayhem The biggest global cultural event of the year may not be something that millions of people watch together but somewhere that millions of people venture separately. In the video game Grand Theft Auto VI, players inhabit a fictionalised America through the eyes of two lovers turned cons in a rags-to-riches crime epic. On Thursday, when the game was released, workers called in sick and students skipped lectures to play at home. Such is GTA VI’s appeal that it is forecast to rake in billions of dollars within months. The game has been billed as a satire of American capitalism, and it is undoubtedly a landmark in interactive storytelling and art. The commercial success of its previous titles has rivalled that of Hollywood blockbusters. Playing GTA VI, as the Guardian’s video games editor observes , is like losing yourself in a doorstop novel, with hours of solitary immersion in a vividly conjured place – not a facsimile of modern Miami, but an interpretation, almost the size of Manchester , rendered with astonishing precision by the artists who designed,

articles.title: Here’s how we can give Neets a fighting chance | Letters
articles.description: Readers respond to Alan Milburn’s plan to tackle the youth jobs crisis Why is Labour reinventing the wheel ( Alan Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people, 16 November )? There is an easier and less discriminatory way – and that is through the mainstream education system. This would not dump these young people into a post-16 Neet silo. Further education (FE) colleges have been working in the area of young people’s training and further education for decades. Yet the sector has been continually undermined by successive governments allowing terrible salary discrimination against the FE sector and by the need to chase numbers (and cash) for A-level-type students. articles.title: Academic integrity matters, but students shouldn’t be penalised for using AI | Letter
articles.description: Berthold Schoene responds after the head of Ofqual said students could be disqualified from GCSEs and A-levels if they tried to use AI in assessed coursework Is this really the best we can do: draconically penalise the young for making use of the latest cognitive resources and tools available to them ( Ofqual urges ‘life-altering’ penalties for students who use tech to cheat, 18 November )? Our generation has allowed the introduction of “life-altering” new technologies into every walk of life without much democratic debate, public scrutiny or governmental oversight. And now our education leaders are threatening to jeopardise young people’s career prospects for deploying these technologies within an education system that can’t cope and struggles to adapt? We all know that AI is here to stay. And importantly, it is so much more than just a cheap cheating device. Within an incredibly short space of time, it has transformed how we work, communicate, solve problems, research and learn. Surely the pedagogical response cannot simply be to devise ever more elaborate ways of preventing students from using it? Continue reading...

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto would be a huge TV series – here’s why it will never happen
articles.description: It is the biggest game of the decade, but there are a billion reasons why GTA shouldn’t be adapted for television. It joins a list of wildly popular titles that won’t see the light of day on streaming platforms You probably aren’t going to see a Grand Theft Auto TV show anytime soon. Speaking on a recent podcast, Strauss Zelnick, the CEO of the game’s parent company Take-Two Interactive, said that a film or television adaptation of GTA would only happen if its team thought that it would “somehow engage and delight our consumers. It’s a high bar to do that. And, of course, there’s always a risk of failure. So we don’t rule it out, but we’re very, very selective.” And, well, good. There are a billion reasons why a small screen version would be a terrible idea. Creatively, the thrill of a GTA game is that no two players have the exact same experience. While you might spend your days mowing down civilians and bazookaing police helicopters out of the skies, someone else might take that time to go hiking or explore the waterways. articles.title: ‘In our lands the rain is made of bullets’: Palestinian artists look back in anger, melancholy and defiance
articles.description: IMMA, Dublin From massacre locations painted on to basalt slabs to photocollages of bulldozed airports, artists from across the Levant address their traumatic history In 2006, Simone Fattal painted on to basalt slabs the names of places indelibly associated with massacres in the Levant since 1948: Deir Yassin; Jenin; Qana; Sabra. Through the names, in the same Arabic script, runs a line of poetry by Etel Adnan: “In our lands of drought the rain forever is made of bullets.” Fattal’s work, which documents atrocities on a material that burst from the earth as lava before settling into stone, introduces a show that likewise combines the recording of history with anger both hot and cold. The last named of those massacres, perpetrated by a Lebanese Christian phalangist militia during Beirut’s occupation by Israeli forces in 1982, also inspired the poem Praise for the High Shadow by Mahmoud Darwish, a line from which this show takes as its title. Writing in exile in Beirut, Darwish riffed on the sea as a symbol of Palestinian displacement and memory, connecting people dispersed around the eastern Mediterranean to each other and to their homeland. The angry, melancholy, defiant work of the

articles.title: Abandoning a Cat by Haruki Murakami review – an intimate meditation on family and memory
articles.description: The author explores the life and legacy of his estranged father, from adoption and abandonment to his horrific experiences of the second world war When Haruki Murakami was a child living in Nishinomiya, Japan, his father announced they were getting rid of their cat. He put his son and the cat on his bike and cycled along the Shukugawa river to a beach 2km from their house. There, they put the box with the cat in it on the ground among some trees and cycled away “without a backward glance”. When they got home, they opened their door to find the cat they’d just left “greeting us with a friendly meow, its tail standing tall. It had beaten us home.” Murakami always wondered how the cat got home so quickly, and why his father had wanted to banish her. These are just some of the unanswered questions that surface in Abandoning a Cat, an essay that first appeared in the New Yorker in 2019, and which is now being published as a book and audiobook. Translated by Philip Gabriel and read with gentle warmth by Kotaro Watanabe, it finds the author telling the story of Murakami Sr, from whom he was estranged for 20 years and who remained a mystery to him in his lifetime. Continue reading...

articles.title: Flottiana album review – 10-cd collection celebrates a very, very great Dame
articles.description: Lott/Johnson (Hyperion) We lost a truly singular talent with the death of Dame Felicity Lott earlier this year. This box-set brings together some of the British soprano’s finest recordings When Dame Felicity Lott died in May this year, the world lost a truly singular talent. An effortlessly elegant soprano, Flott, as she was known, was as at home in German, and especially French, as she was in her native English. This 10-CD boxset from Hyperion brings together some of her finest recordings from a career that spanned half a century. It’s curated by Graham Johnson, who in 1976 recruited Lott for The Songmakers’ Almanac, the pioneering vocal ensemble whose mission was to explore neglected corners of the repertoire. First, the voice; an instrument that appears incapable of anything indecorous. It never spreads or strays from the note, maintaining a purity and brilliance even when hovering in the musical stratosphere. Then there’s the diction, crisp and clear, wedded to an intelligence that lays bare the inner meaning of a song without mannerisms or affectation. With Lott it was straight and to the point, every emotion subtly and honestly conveyed. Continue reading...

articles.title: James McAvoy’s random encounter triggers a delusional fantasy in Parasocial Activity
articles.description: Òran Mór, Glasgow In Briony Martha’s compelling play, a woman generates an alternative ending to her impromptu meeting with the Scottish superstar Knowing what to believe is getting harder. Technology has blurred the line between truth and lies. Certain facts, though, we can demonstrate. We know, for example, that James McAvoy appeared in Cyrano de Bergerac at the Theatre Royal in Glasgow in the mask-wearing spring of 2022. We can also take playwright Briony Martha at her word when she says she bumped into the actor in a nearby coffee shop. It is even true that McAvoy was in the audience of Martha’s Parasocial Activity towards the end of this summer’s run on the Edinburgh fringe: a performance that can only have had a heightened air of unreality. At Òran Mór, Glasgow , until 21 November. At Southwark Playhouse, London , 13-30 January. Continue reading...

articles.title: Jeff Buckley was a 90s indie darling. Now gen Z think he’s the ‘yearner final boss’
articles.description: With his unguarded lyricism and earnest delivery, the late singer-songwriter is having a moment among a generation that fetishizes unrequited desire Sydney Tripoli has collected Jeff Buckley memorabilia since 2019. She keeps her collection of T-shirts, posters, vinyl and other merch celebrating the late singer-songwriter in what she affectionately calls her “Buckley box”. The 27-year-old scours eBay and resale sites for these pieces; lately she’s noticed the prices “skyrocket”. “During the pandemic, it was impossible to find Jeff Buckley shirts. Now they’re everywhere on Depop,” said Tripoli, who works as an actor in Los Angeles. “Now [my collection] is worth thousands of dollars.” Continue reading...

articles.title: The best early UK Black Friday deals on the products we love, from heated airers to the perfect pillow
articles.description: We’ve cut through the noise to find genuinely good early Black Friday 2026 discounts on Filter-tested products across home, kitchen, fitness, beauty and more • The best sustainable Black Friday deals Retailers aren’t rolling out their Black Friday discounts from the kindness of their hearts. It’s business. But if you can resist the urge to impulse-buy anything with a red ticket, and instead focus your attention on genuinely discounted items that you genuinely want, then it’s a potentially big win for you, too. The whole shebang lasts a fortnight these days, but it’s not quite in full swing yet. At the time of writing, the actual Friday in question (27 November) is just over a week away, and many of the best deals haven’t landed yet. Plenty of brands have been at it for days, though, with John Lewis, Boots and, inevitably, Amazon launching their Black Friday sales when you could still smell fireworks in the air. Continue reading...

articles.title: How beaujolais conquered the snobs
articles.description: Beaujolais is enjoying something of a renaissance, with even much-maligned nouveau gaining ground thanks to the fashion for light, chilled, low-tannin reds “Oh, it’s beaujolais. Fantastic!” My earliest memory of beaujolais isn’t of drinking it, but of saying it, on stage, as Beverley in a school production of Mike Leigh’s Abigail’s Party . Leigh wrote the play a few years into the British craze for beaujolais nouveau, the just-made, casual quaffing wine – historically destined for local consumption in France – that’s released on the third Thursday of every November. Sold cheaply, it landed beaujolais with an image that belied its extraordinary variety and quality. It was, says The Encyclopedia of Wine , “a self-administered cataclysm” on beaujolais’ part. Nowadays, it’s common knowledge that there is more to beaujolais than beaujolais nouveau, from its most famous village crus, such as Fleurie, Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent, to higher-altitude, lesser-known villages that, amid the climate crisis, are now coming into their own. Beaujolais lies just south of Burgundy, in the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region, with mostly granite-based soils to the north (perfectly suited to the red gamay grape

articles.title: I’m engaged but I can’t stop thinking about an old friend. Should I tell him how I feel? | Leading questions
articles.description: Telling him would risk a lot of harm, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. If you’re going to take that gamble, you’d better be sure why you’re doing it Read more Leading questions My partner and I are engaged after a whirlwind romance, and I was over the moon when he proposed. He is a wonderful, kind and generous man, and will be an amazing husband. However, I’ve since found out that a friend I’ve known for years has always carried a torch for me, and this knowledge has made me see him in a different light. I can’t stop thinking about him, and it’s making me question if I should marry my fiance. My friend has no idea I feel this way, and has recently got engaged, so nothing has obviously changed, apart from my feelings. Do I continue with planning my wedding and push these new feelings down, or do I tell my friend how I feel in case he still feels the same? This indecision is torturing me. Continue reading...

articles.description: AI startup and Claude chatbot maker became one of the world’s most valuable publicly traded businesses with final share price of $97 Anthropic closed its first day of trading on the US stock market about 17% higher than its initial public offering price. At the close of market on Thursday, Anthropic shares were trading at just over $97 with a nearly $1.3tn total market capitalization, $1.75tn fully diluted. While the final share value was higher than the IPO price of $83, it marked a dip from an early high of $111.50. The firm’s shares initially soared 34% when trading got under way on its US market debut on Thursday, valuing the company at more than $2tn.
