articles.title: Terror on Bondi Beach review – these astounding stories recreate every single second of horror
articles.description: From agonised parents trying to find their children, to the man who tackled a gunman – these gripping accounts of the 2025 Sydney attacks should never be forgotten Milo Riley-Smith’s documentary is a simple piece of diligent work. It begins by spending a short time gathering the backstories of its interviewees: how they or their parents came to Australia seeking a new life, finding it to be a welcoming place where, as one woman remembers, Jews “could have a fair go” because anyone could, whatever their ethnicity. These Jewish Australians then talk about how, after Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack on Israel and Israel’s subsequent bombardment of Gaza, they began to feel less safe. They had seen a flaring of antisemitic violence, vandalism and rhetoric; they attended the annual Hanukah festivities at Sydney’s Bondi beach with some trepidation. After an extended account of the events of 14 December 2025, the documentary’s participants comment briefly on whether enough was done by the Australian authorities to protect them. Continue reading...

articles.title: Sandpapergate has gone from a sporting scandal to a rolling loop of outrage and overreaction | Jonathan Horn
articles.description: Nothing about the responses and reprisals to Australia’s ball tampering have been proportional in a story where the truth probably lies somewhere in the middle Who said long-form journalism is dead? As Matt Renshaw nudged his ones and twos in an already forgotten ODI match, the broadcasters were scanning Cameron Bancroft’s 4000-word essay . SEN’s Gerard Whateley was calling for a comprehensive judicial inquiry, “a little bit like a coroner’s inquest,” with witnesses compelled to attend and be subjected to cross examination. Cricket Australia’s “forum” , announced a few hours earlier, had already been skittled. Nothing in the eight years since a piece of sandpaper was taken on to the field in Cape Town, including the publication of Usman Khawaja’s book Sabr , had been as revelatory as Bancroft’s first-person account . But as always with this story, we were bracing for the next press conference, the next podcast, the next corroborating statement, the next counterclaim, the next overreaction. Continue reading...

articles.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
articles.description: Bruno Guimarães to feel the heat on Tyneside, Alex Scott’s return further cheers Cherries and Manchester City face favourite whipping boys After three Premier League defeats on the spin, Manchester City need something or someone to come along and put some pep in their step, and Fulham look like just the thing – after all, in the past 15 years these teams have played 20 times in all competitions, and City have won precisely 20 of those games. Their current run of 17 successive league wins against Fulham is the longest run of victories by one club against a single opponent in English top-flight history. It is a reflection of the changing realities of English football, and the gulf that has opened between the teams that dominate it and those who seek to challenge them, that of the top 10 such runs all but one occurred in whole or in part after 2010 and six of them have been achieved by Sheikh Mansour’s Manchester City, with Chelsea responsible for another two, Manchester United one, and Portsmouth’s postwar, 13-game supremacy over Everton – a wild ride that included two 5-0s, a 5-1, a 6-3 and a 7-0 – the anomaly. Simon Burnton Manchester City v Fulham, Saturday 12.30pm (all times GMT)

articles.title: Belfast Flood Alleviation Scheme Sept 14-18
articles.description: Belfast Tidal Flood Alleviation Scheme Training Exercise A training exercise to install the temporary defences will take place between 14 – 18 September 2026. This year the locations are: Harbour Estate Sydenham (Greggs Quay to The O2 Belfast) Sydenham (Pottinger's Quay) Ravenhill As part of the exercise, the slip road from Ravenhill Road to the Albert Bridge will be closed overnight between 11pm and 6am on Wednesday 16 September. If required , the closure may also be in place on Thursday 17 September again overnight between 11pm and 6am. Diversion signage will be provided, directing city centre-bound traffic via Bridge End and Queen's Bridge. There may also be some short-term disruption and temporary footpath closures at other locations. Advisory signs will be provided where necessary, including along the towpath. The Department would like to thank the public in advance for their patience. Further details, including locations and programme, are available at: Belfast Tidal Flood Alleviation Scheme | Department for Infrastructure .

articles.title: NI Water Works - Cornagrade Road Enniskillen 3 Aug
articles.description: Essential Water Infrastructure Improvement Work gets underway – Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen NI Water is set to commence an upgrade of the water infrastructure on Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen in early August for approximately 6 weeks. The work will see around 400m of new watermain being laid along Cornagrade Road, starting at Cherrymount Roundabout on Monday 3 rd August and progressing as far as the second entrance to Kilmacormick Road. To facilitate the laying of this new watermain, a lane closure will be in place around each working area and signage will be in place. Working areas will be kept as short as possible (around 100m) with temporary traffic lights in place to manage the flow of traffic. Access to residential and business properties on and adjacent to Cornagrade Road will be available at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be affected for a short period of time while the pipelaying passes. Any bus stop located within a working area will be temporarily relocated.

articles.title: Derry - NIW Scheme - Racecourse Rd - from 27 July
articles.description: Essential water network upgrade to get underway on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett NI Water is set to begin an essential watermain upgrade on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett (Derry/Londonderry) on Monday 27 th July to improve the resilience of the local water supply network. The work, which involves laying around 170 metres of new watermain between Carnhill Roundabout and Greenhaw Road, will replace a section of the 50-year-old Ballyarnett Water Trunkmain which has been prone to bursts. The upgrade will help to protect homes from flooding, should a burst occur in the future, and provide improved access for NI Water maintenance. A l ane closure controlled by temporary traffic lights will be in place on Racecourse Road around the working area from Monday 27 th July for four weeks. A further two weeks of work will take place in the adjacent verge which will not require any traffic management. Temporary traffic lights will be manned during peak hours and access to properties will be maintained at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be temporarily unavailable. Once the lane closure is removed, works will move into the adjacent verge to complete the final phase of w

articles.title: Craigavon - Closure of Maple Path & Parkmore Footbridges
articles.description: Closure of Maple Path and Parkmore Footbridges, Craigavon The Department for Infrastructure have announced that the Maple Path and Parkmore footbridges in Craigavon will be closed from Thursday 4 June 2026. Detailed engineering inspections identified structural concerns, and it has been concluded that the closure of these footbridges is necessary while a permanent solution is developed. Alternative local walking routes are available and will be signposted where appropriate. While these routes may increase journey times for some users, they will provide access around the affected areas. The Department recognises the importance of both footbridges to local residents and apologises for any inconvenience caused. However, as the Department’s infrastructure assets age there will always be an eventual need to replace structures that present safety issues or have come to the end of their natural lifespan. Further information on future proposals for the bridges will be provided as work progresses. The Department would like to thank the public for their patience and cooperation.

articles.description: Rep. In a live feed, the Kentucky Republican issued the impeachment articles on the floor of the US House of Representatives ahead of a scheduled press conference Monday afternoon. It was not yet clear when a vote will take place but it is supposed to happen within the next two days under House rules. It will be the first major vote since Democrats’ landslide victory in the midterms last week. articles.description: AI Is Outrunning America's Cyber Defenses, And Washington Has No Plan To Catch Up Two senators, one Democrat and one Republican, warned the Trump administration on Wednesday that AI-enabled cyber threats are "rapidly escalating" and outpacing America's defenses . Sens. Maria Cantwell (D-WA) and Mike Rounds (R-SD) sent the warning in a letter to Jay Clayton, chair of the White House Super Intelligence Task Force. They urged immediate action to protect critical infrastructure, financial institutions and widely used software. The letter follows a week of technology failures that reached airports, tech companies, media, and even banks. A Microsoft outage took down email and other services. U.S. air travel came to a halt . A software problem at JPMorgan Chase hit banking services. The administration has rejected the idea that foreign hackers caused the disruptions. Instead, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has pointed to artificial intelligence as a possible cause, including the problem that grounded every U.S. flight for hours last week. "I am the chief accountability officer. I take full responsibility for it," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said regarding the ground stop. Some records also contained phone numbers and account IDs. The Reserve card is a Visa product for high-net-worth clients, typically associated with at least $10 million in assets managed by the bank, according to Cybernews. The outlet said the released dataset was only 502 KB , and it was unclear whether it represented a sample or everything the attackers had stolen. articles.description: Denmark Unanimously Ratifies Trump's Greenland Deal, Opening Door To Golden Dome Authored by Tom Ozimek via The Epoch Times , Lawmakers in Denmark - which administers Greenland - on Thursday approved a security agreement between the Arctic island and the United States to bolster security. The deal, which U.S. President Donald Trump signed in September with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland, was formally ratified in a Nov. 19 vote in the Danish parliament, with 109 lawmakers voting for and none against. With their vote, Danish lawmakers gave parliamentary consent to an agreement between Greenland, Denmark and the United States that amends a 1951 agreement on Greenland's defense, established under the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO). While the 1951 agreement already granted the United States sweeping military rights in Greenland, the new deal strengthens certain access rights and allows the United States to expand its military footprint on the Arctic island . articles.description: Continuing Jobless Claims Unexpectedly Jump As 'Low Hire, Low Fire, Low Inspire' Economy Rolls On Last week we called it the labor market's trilemma: claims at 57-year lows, sentiment near record lows and a hires rate stuck at 3.4% (Nov 12). This morning the "low fire" leg finally blinked. Not by much, but in the wrong direction, and just as the Fed has decided to keep hiking. In his latest US Daily note, titled "US Daily: Adding A Third Hike" ( available to pro subs ), Goldman economist David Mericle expects a second 25bp hike in December and a third in March 2027, with the first cut pushed out to December 2027. In other words, Goldman reads these data as a labor market strong enough to tighten into , and a consumer about to pay for it. Eight Weeks, Not Nine Start with the headline. Initial jobless claims printed 203K for the week ended Nov 14 against 198K expected, and last week's 200K was revised up to 202K . The four-week average rose 2,000 to 197,750. articles.description: Harvard Study Reveals What Happens When Schools Lock Up Kids' Phones Shocker... Schools that locked students' phones away for the whole school day saw math and reading scores grow faster , by about one to two extra weeks of learning a year, according to a Harvard study of 3.3 million students released Tuesday. The study , from Harvard's Center for Education Policy Research, followed students at 4,600 schools from the 2021-22 through the 2025-26 school years. Strict bans - lockable Yondr-style pouches, phones stored centrally, or phones kept off campus altogether - raised annual achievement growth by about 0.01 standard deviations , roughly half of what students have been losing each year since smartphones went mainstream. articles.description: Stunning Moment "World's Most Endangered Tribe" Makes Rare Contact With Outsiders Members of the Awá tribe, dubbed the "world's most endangered tribe ," have stunned villagers after emerging from the depths of the Brazilian rainforest in a rare encounter with the outside world. Roughly 20 members of the isolated Indigenous group, including women and children, approached a government outpost in Brazil's northeastern Maranhão state on Monday , marking their first known encounter of this kind in decades, Reuters reports. The group reportedly asked for yams before disappearing back into the forest with their food, according to Survival International . The Indigenous rights organization warned that illegal loggers, hunters and cattle ranchers have been steadily destroying the tribe's ancestral hunting grounds. "This is a troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples' forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger," said the organization's director, Caroline Pearce. "She had been knowingly giving him secret information. The reason she did it is because she thought he was in love with her. He wasn't," recalled Thomas Lee Boam, a U.S. diplomat stationed in East Germany at the time. The secretary went to prison and has since been released. In intelligence parlance, the tactic has an enduring name: the "honey trap" - known in Chinese as the "beauty trap." "Oh, that happens all the time," Boam told The Epoch Times. "The government sends a very attractive person, male or female depending on the American [target], to engage in a relationship with that person. And it's so common, it has a name. articles.title: Electoral College Under Threat
articles.description: Electoral College Under Threat Authored by Joseph Burns via City Journal , With the 2026 election in the books, attention turns to what emboldened Democrats from state capitals to Capitol Hill will do with their newfound power. The press appears focused on hot topics like AI and affordability policies. But another item that could be on Democrats' agenda - and has received almost no media attention - may have an even greater impact on the nation's future. For the better part of the last two decades, far-left activists have pushed the idea of abolishing the Electoral College, not through the obvious route of a constitutional amendment but instead through the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact (NPVIC) . The proposal attempts to undermine the Constitution by having states pledge their electors to the winner of the national popular vote, regardless of how the states voted. The compact, however, would take effect only when enough states to represent a majority of the Electoral College agree to it. That's what makes the results of the 2026 election so important. articles.title: Killer tunes: how Grand Theft Auto conquered the music world
articles.description: Featuring hundreds of songs from the hippest real-world artists, the radio stations in Rockstar’s crime sagas are as hotly anticipated as the storylines. Contributors including Flying Lotus, Wavves and Nite Jewel reflect on the soundtracks’ curation and impact • The exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI • Crime pays: how GTA became a cultural colossus • Ten movies (and one TV show) that inspired GTA A droptop sports car speeds along a highway blaring 90s west coast rap from its booming sound system. Gradually, the asphalt gives way to rural backwaters, and so the sounds of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas’s local radio also change: less gangster rap and more twangin’ country – the grizzled croon of Merle Haggard and yearning warble of Patsy Cline. The Grand Theft Auto games are massive, stretching across many, many square miles of virtual terrain. Their soundtracks, relayed mostly via in-game radio stations, are manifold. And these two aspects, plus the personal experiences each player brings to the game, mean everyone has a different favourite musical memory from the smash-hit crime series. For acclaimed electronic musician Flying Lotus, it is all the hours he spent cavorting

articles.title: They’re one of the UK’s greatest cult bands – who swore they’d never reunite. What brought Life Without Buildings back together?
articles.description: The Scottish quartet existed for just three years at the turn of the millennium. But after Frank Ocean and TikTok thrilled to Sue Tompkins’ unique vocals, they’re back. They explain their fears about ‘spoiling the joy’ ‘I’m excited, I’m scared, I’m anxious – that bubbling feeling, like when you’re on a rollercoaster, at the very top, just before the big drop.” On a drizzly afternoon in July, huddled with her three bandmates in the cramped cupboard that’s the dressing room of Glasgow venue Mono, Sue Tompkins is managing her feelings ahead of her first proper gig with Life Without Buildings in almost a quarter of a century. “Everybody coming is invited, it’s secret, nobody paid much to get in, the profits are going to charity,” adds guitarist Robert Dallas Gray, sat beside her, as much to steady his own nerves as to explain the circumstances of tonight’s show. “I hope people aren’t looking at it like we’re fucking entertainers .” Continue reading...

articles.title: The 45 best Secret Santa gifts in the UK for £15 or less – tried and tested for 2026
articles.description: From grippy socks and posh condiments to beautiful stationery and accessories, these affordable Christmas presents are anything but naff • The best Christmas gifts for 2026 Secret Santa is an amazing concept to reduce the amount of gifts you feel obliged to buy, but I find it can result in quite a bit of tat. Resist the urge to buy a joke gift – often instant landfill – and use your budget to get your recipient something useful, or that feels quite treat-y. I’m assuming for this guide that the rules of Secret Santa are that you know who your recipient is – they just don’t know who the gift is from. That is helpful as you can tailor it to their tastes and hobbies. If it’s blind both ways, food is always well received, and socks – while a Christmas cliche – are something everyone wants a new pair of (just get the best you can afford, not, as one of my family used to do, just restock my black school socks). Continue reading...

At the time, the US president had enlisted the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, to run his “department of government efficiency” (Doge). During a 16-week blitz at the heart of the US government , Musk caused chaos, fired tens of thousands of workers and gutted USAID. Continue reading...

articles.title: The best Christmas baubles in the UK: 26 quirky decorations, from a velvet turnip to a Suffragette mouse
articles.description: Bored of red and gold? This year’s tree trimmings are felted, beaded and handmade – and they’re all glitter-free • The best artificial Christmas trees – tested Baubles: every time we think we’ve reached peak wackiness, we’re proved wrong the following year. On the menu for 2026 are food and drink ornaments, with everything from Guinness to gildas; felt animals with imaginative personalities, jobs and political agendas (see the suffragette mouse); and retro-inspired ornaments, including a cute gramophone. And we couldn’t resist a handmade decoration paying tribute to the late, great Amy Winehouse. Here are our favourites, and they’re all glitter-free. *** Continue reading...

articles.title: Doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby was barred from treating patients during trial
articles.description: Exclusive: Jury was never told that Prof Peter Hindmarsh was barred from practising over concerns for patients’ safety A senior doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby and who was held up by prosecutors as a pre-eminent expert was barred from treating patients during the trial over fears he posed a risk to their safety. Prof Peter Hindmarsh, a specialist in hormones in children, was crucial to the crown’s argument that the British nurse had poisoned children by injecting insulin into fluid bags. But a Guardian investigation can reveal he was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023, five months before the end of the trial, by his employer, University College London hospitals trust (UCLH). Jurors were never told. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘They want silence’: how the film NAZA is shaking Israel
articles.description: The documentary has triggered fierce backlash, but by exposing the army’s conduct in Gaza it’s proved impossible to ignore It was on Yom Kippur this year that Nadav Weiman first sensed the documentary NAZA was having a significant impact in Israel – despite the fact that back in September, when the Jewish festival fell, barely a handful of Israelis had seen the film. NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and will stream for free on its website in early December, depicts 24 army intelligence officers interviewed anonymously on rooftops across Tel Aviv. They talk about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza over the past three years, and the secret signoff system employed by Israel’s military. More than 1.5 million people have already seen it in cinemas and its Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor have picked up a roster of prestigious awards. The film has been offered to a number of distributors and cinemas in Israel but has not been screened there yet, amid a severe backlash. Continue reading...

articles.title: Van Eyck: The Portraits review – a jewel box of phenomenal death-defeating paintings
articles.description: National Gallery, London Bringing together all the pioneering master’s portraits for the first time reveals the way he clinically preserved monsters, merchants – even his wife – like flies in amber Tricks! Traps! Riddles! Jan van Eyck’s portraits look vividly real – but are full of secret messages. What do they mean? The stubble is tiny yet silver-sharp on the chin of an unknown old man whom Jan van Eyck painted in oils 600 years ago: so long after both are dead you can still see this bloke needs a shave. The hairs on top of his head are just as miraculously caught, varying individually in paleness and lankness. You feast your eyes on the sagging skin of his throat with its overhangs and shady gulleys like a rock formation. He is a wonder, a freak of nature and yet a perfectly ordinary person. So are we all banal and marvellous, mundane and impossible, suggests Van Eyck. The National Gallery has created a jewel box of a show bringing together all Van Eyck’s portraits as we define them – a painting of a person for its own sake. Yet portraitist was a long way from being his only job. Van Eyck painted stupendous religious works, including the Ghent Altarpiece that he collaborated on w

articles.title: Cosimo I de’Medici review – up close and personal with a Renaissance godfather
articles.description: Wallace Collection, London A sword, a wine cooler, a dazzling fresco … only a museum with such a copious store of treasures could put on a display this rich without having to borrow Mounting a “store-cupboard” exhibition – choosing items from existing collections to make a new, contained display – can be a cheap and easy way for a museum to make something out of its existing resources, without the faff of securing loans or collaborating across the industry. In the case of the Wallace Collection, however, the store cupboard is so embarrassingly rich and diverse that strong displays such as this on Cosimo I de’Medici can be drawn from only a handful of its objects. The 19th-century collection of Sir Richard Wallace holds a notable number of medieval objects, but their display can seem – at least to contemporary eyes – like a cacophony of applied arts, armour and paintings, not to mention a ton of gilt. This Medici display is part of a new enterprise drawing out histories from the noise for singular focus, sensibly repurposing what was once the cloakroom (a previously wasted bit of prime real estate) as a new dedicated space. Continue reading...

articles.title: How to deal with a class difference in friendships? Make fun of your privileged friends
articles.description: Lasting cross-class friendships involve routinely ‘taking the piss’ out of the more privileged party, research by the LSE shows Routinely “taking the piss” out of more privileged friends is one of the main ways people cope with a class difference in their friendships, research has found. Cross-class friendships are widespread and mutually beneficial, a study by the London School of Economics showed, but a class gap can still pose an “omnipresent threat” to friendships. Continue reading...

articles.description: Diplomats say piecemeal approach of resets is coming to an end and Europe wants clarity on whether Britain wants to reverse its exit The EU will shut the door to discussions with Andy Burnham about the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc until the government has decided whether it wants to proceed with reversing Brexit, diplomats have said. articles.title: World ‘held hostage by oil mafia’, says Panama minister at Cop 31
articles.description: Key issues unresolved as summit enters final days, with 30 countries signed up to forge fossil fuel treaty separate to UN process The world is “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia” and seems unable to break free, Panama’s environment minister has warned, as key issues remain unresolved in the final days of the UN Cop31 climate summit . “We are in love with our kidnappers,” said Juan Carlos Navarro, at a press conference to announce 30 countries were now signed up to forge a new fossil fuel treaty, separate to the UN process. “We love the petroleum guys. We can’t live without them, and they are so smart they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good.” Continue reading...

articles.title: A TikTok superstar bares all: Siorna Ashby’s best shot
articles.description: Portraits often rely on the face and eyes to communicate. Here, I wanted to explore how much of Meg’s presence and personality could come through her body and gesture I met Meg at a nude life-drawing class. I was struck by how free she seemed and how powerfully that came through in her modelling. I asked if I could photograph her for my project Body Like Mine. This series explores the difference between how our bodies are perceived externally and how we experience them ourselves. We see a body and we bring our own judgments and assumptions on to it, but the lived experience is very different. Rather than portraying an idealised body, the project aims to explore what it feels like to inhabit your own body, and to see it as worthy of attention without asking it to become anything else first. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on the Trump, Xi and Putin meeting: it may be a first, but it’s not progress | Editorial
articles.description: A trilateral gathering is good news for China and Russia, but bad for the US – and its traditional allies “Historic” is a neutral descriptor, not a favourable one. Things can be unprecedented for good reason. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Thursday will be the first time that the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio. The trilateral on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is striking, but it is not an achievement. The lack of a clear agenda is telling: the spectacle really is the substance. Mr Trump sees international affairs in terms of spheres of influence. This meeting reinforces the obvious conclusion for the rest of the world – that they don’t get to sit at the table, only to be on the plate. Mr Xi promotes the notion of a multipolar world. Others would be more sympathetic if all three governments were not determinedly undermining multilateralism. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here . Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on ‘two-tier policing’: tackle the myth, don’t pander to it | Editorial
articles.description: Confidence in the system is being corroded by cynical campaigns and far-right propaganda – that is the challenge to be confronted There are many areas of policy where public opinion diverges from evidence. Voters overestimate rates of crime, for example. Many will be sceptical of politicians who say today’s streets are safer than they used to be, although that is the reality. The challenge is to find methods of persuasion that don’t belittle the experiences of people who are afraid, and don’t like to be told their fears are unfounded. But there is a different challenge that arises when the cause of public concern is a problem that doesn’t really exist. Many people are angry about “ two-tier policing ” in Britain, supposedly characterised by disproportionately severe enforcement against white people and leniency towards minorities. There is no evidence to support a systemic bias of that kind. By contrast, the data suggests an imbalance of fair treatment goes the other way. People of colour are underrepresented in the police, disproportionately targeted with stop-and-search policies and, if arrested, likelier to have force used against them. Do you have an opinion on the issues raise

articles.title: Why Palantir’s health tech is not the right fit for the NHS | Letter
articles.description: The US firm’s health data system is based on an insurance model of healthcare, not the patient-centred universal service we have in Britain, says Prof Caroline Mitchell The news that NHS England may have overstated the benefits of Palantir for improving efficiency will surprise few frontline clinicians ( NHS England deletes ‘misleading’ claim 137 trusts benefiting from Palantir AI tools, 12 November ) Too often, global digital policy assumes that software designed for the fragmented, insurance-based US healthcare system can simply be adapted to a universal public service elsewhere. A legitimate concern is that algorithms underpinning AI decision-making may be immature in the NHS context, having been developed primarily for a very different US healthcare system. Continue reading...

articles.title: Blaming Ofsted inspectors for the system is unfair | Letters
articles.description: Inspectors and educators alike have been placed under even greater pressure year after year, says Helen Kenny As national officer for the FDA, the union representing a large number of His Majesty’s Inspectors (HMIs), I read Simon Jenkins’ piece with great interest ( Ofsted’s menacing inspections are still disastrous. Schools should answer to the communities they serve, 13 November ). Jenkins dismisses the work of HMIs as merely a “sniff” of the air and a stroll back to Whitehall, showing a lack of knowledge about their role. HMIs are former school leaders, with a deep knowledge and dedication to educating children and young people. They are as far from the typical civil servant (if there is such a thing) that it is possible to get, and in any case are not based in Whitehall. Jenkins does at least suggest an alternative approach, unlike some who are calling for the abolition of Ofsted, but I really question whether he has thought it through. Parents value the provision of inspection, and most educators agree that assessments are fair – independent YouGov polling showed that 74% of educators believed their most recent inspection was accurate. Continue reading...

articles.title: What stops us building the houses Britain needs | Letters
articles.description: Emeritus professor Simon Price , Smart Growth UK’s Jon Reeds and former Labour council leader Steve Siddon respond to a column by John Harris John Harris points out the utter inadequacy of Labour’s housing plans, despite Andy Burnham’s passionate advocacy for new social housing ( Is Burnham’s plan for a housing revolution anything more than a pipedream?, 15 November ). And everyone agrees that we need many more houses. So what’s holding us back? The problem lies in the fiscal rules. At first sight this is puzzling, as borrowing to invest is explicitly allowed (as opposed to borrowing to cover current expenditure). The explanation is the future debt target. Any capital investment increases public debt, and there is a binding debt-to-GDP ratio at the arbitrary and relatively close forecast horizon. Continue reading...

articles.title: BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health | Letter
articles.description: Clinicians should start with the patient in front of them to identify obesity, not rely on a 200-year-old method that was aimed at entire populations, says James Capon Your report on a better way to diagnose obesity is welcome, though it is worth remembering how we came to rely on body mass index (BMI) in the first place ( BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’, 11 November ). The index was devised in the 1830s by the Belgian statistician Adolphe Quetelet, who wanted to describe the “average man” across whole populations. He never intended it as a verdict on any individual’s health, and it was largely forgotten until 1972, when the American physiologist Ancel Keys, most famous for developing the diet-heart hypothesis, revived it and gave it its current name. Again, it was for population studies. Continue reading...

articles.title: How to turn the dregs of an instant coffee jar into a brilliant vegan cake – recipe | Waste not
articles.description: Instant coffee granules are a great ingredient in baking, as shown in this sponge given extra depth from roast walnuts and cardamom-infused milk It might taste subpar in the cup, but instant coffee is a great baking ingredient. Being dehydrated, it provides an intense coffee flavour without adding extra liquid, which often upsets the balance of a recipe. I don’t drink instant coffee myself, and the dregs of the jar we always seem to have at the back of the cupboard tend to grow old and stick together. They’re still good to use, though, and can be chipped off or even dissolved in the jar, if need be. Continue reading...

articles.title: Vincent van Gogh painting auctioned for record $190.4m after dispute over Nazi era sale
articles.description: Chataigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Blossom), which was painted in 1890 in Auvers-sur-Oise, France, set a new record for the Dutch post-impressionist A Vincent van Gogh masterpiece sold for a record-breaking $190.4m (£144.9m, A$285m) on Wednesday after a dispute between the seller and the heirs of a previous Jewish owner who sold it in the Nazi era, Sotheby’s said. articles.title: ‘When it roars, we roar back’: the man who faces Bengal tigers armed only with a stick

articles.title: Outages, spies, and trillion-dollar IPOs: is this our AI future? – Stateside with Kai and Carter
articles.description: It has been a wild few weeks in the world of tech. First, Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, forced an unimaginable leadership change at Nvidia – arguably the most consequential company in AI development. Then, chaos erupted as a rolling set of IT outages disrupted flights, banking, tech companies and the federal government. And now, Anthropic is blowing minds with a trillion-dollar IPO – one of the largest in stock market history. The Atlantic’s tech writer Charlie Warzel tells Kai Wright that these events are linked: they’re all examples of the ways in which we shoulder unprecedented risk today, in order to bet on AI’s future reward. It’s a convoluted logic that keeps the AI race speeding forward, no matter how many warning signs it blows past. Charlie Warzel is also host of the Atlantic’s podcast Galaxy Brain . articles.title: Mentors, colleagues and friends: tributes paid to the ‘Eritrea 16’ who disappeared 25 years ago
articles.description: Families of journalists who vanished into state prisons on ‘Black Tuesday’ in 2001 do not know whether they are even still alive When Fisseha Yirgalem stepped on to the podium and began reading from a letter written to a man who may never hear it, the room full of journalists in Nairobi fell quiet. The Eritrean writer’s personal tribute to Amanuel Asrat , a poet, writer, and founder of Zemen newspaper, was not merely about an abstract human rights case but about her mentor, former colleague and friend whose life had in effect been erased by the authoritarian state of Eritrea. That is something we believe the Ethiopian experience can showcase.” Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Sam-Bankman Fried messaged me from prison’: rising star Anthony Boyle on playing the disgraced tech bro – and a zero-hours bike courier
articles.description: The actor’s latest roles see him go from a delivery guy on £40 a day to the notorious crypto scammer who stole more than $10bn. His sympathies are clear: ‘I wasn’t brought up to care about money,’ he says In the spring of 2019, Anthony Boyle went to see Cillian Murphy in Grief Is the Thing with Feathers at St Ann’s Warehouse in Brooklyn. Afterwards, the 24-year-old actor hung around the stage door. “There were 500 people queueing up for Cillian, but I was the only one who wanted to meet Enda Walsh,” says Boyle, laughing. When the Dublin-born writer Walsh finally appeared, Boyle introduced himself. He was from west Belfast, he’d read Walsh’s plays at drama school, and it was his dream to work with him one day. He asked if Walsh would like to come and see him on Broadway, where he was playing Scorpius Malfoy, son of Draco, in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. How did he respond? Boyle grins. “He was sort of like: ‘Oh.’” Since Walsh never went to see The Cursed Child, Boyle assumed the writer had immediately forgotten about him. articles.title: Bank your stolen cash, bring a change of clothes, go easy on the bloodshed: 15 tips for playing Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.description: There’s a vast amount to absorb in Leonida, but these pointers will rev up your criminal engines and allow you to better enjoy the ride Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? Leonida is so huge as to be overwhelming and in the opening hours, the game bombards you with tonnes of info that you will inevitably forget. But I’ve done nothing but play this game for weeks and I’m here to help. Here’s what I wished I’d known at the start Walk faster. I found that Jason and Lucia walk incredibly slowly. articles.title: Ram through datacentres no one wants and hope the AI bubble never bursts: that’s the UK’s growth plan | George Monbiot
articles.description: The government doesn’t know what they are going to be used for, but that’s beside the point. Their real purpose is to sustain the share price of big tech It should have the status of an economic law: the sectors a government does most to promote in the name of growth are the sectors most likely to tank the economy. In the UK and the US, deregulation was meant to turn the financial sector into a never-ending growth machine. We have not yet fully recovered from the crash it helped cause in 2008. Fossil fuels are the most heavily subsidised sector on Earth. All that public money makes us highly vulnerable to oil price shocks, the whims of autocrats and societal collapse caused by climate breakdown. As for the great growth priority of our time – AI and datacentres – well, don’t take it from me. As Anthropic’s IPO prospectus warns , advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”. One thing we learned from the US midterm elections is that the drive to build datacentres is less a function of real commercial demand than of the need to sustain the share price of the big tech companies. After citizens across the US voted for moratoria on new datacentres, tech

articles.title: Teachers want to prepare pupils for post-16 life. This is why it’s so difficult | Lola Okolosie
articles.description: I welcome Alan Milburn’s call for schools to focus more on students’ potential beyond exams. Yet I must ask: where is the money? At 16, life should feel like a path leading to endless opportunities. That is at least the carrot dangled in front of young people to motivate them through the gruelling years of exam preparation. “Your life starts now,” their teachers all but tell them. And though for the vast majority that is true, there is a cohort who are forced to accept that the bright futures they were promised are beyond their reach. They are the nearly one million young people aged between 16 and 24 who are not in education, employment or training (Neets). Alan Milburn’s second report on the nation’s Neets places schools at the heart of the solution. It proposes that schools should be judged not only on grades but also whether pupils continue their post-16 journey into further education or work. Technical education, it also argues, must be regarded with the same gravitas as the academic. Most people working in education won’t argue with this rationale. As ever, the sticking point is how it is to be funded. Lola Okolosie is an English teacher and writer Continue reading...

articles.title: You have to laugh at LIV’s collapse but the saga reveals money is golf’s core value | Jonathan Liew
articles.description: Why do rich powerful men love golf? Ultimately the sport exists in a world where the politics is assumed to be settled Farewell, then, LIV Golf. As its original figurehead Greg Norman once so delicately put it, albeit in a slightly different context: we’ve all made mistakes, you learn from those mistakes, and you move forward. Forward – in LIV’s case – to bankruptcy court and the start of liquidation proceedings some time in January 2027. And not without a certain irony, in the sense that Norman’s cherished project, established over a cacophony of human rights concerns, ended up getting dismembered and terminated on the orders of the Saudi government. Life moves on you pretty fast. Perhaps the funniest part of LIV’s protracted demise – unless you count the television viewing figures – has been the last seven months, after Saudi Arabia abruptly pulled the plug on the seemingly abundant flow of money that had fuelled its astonishing rise. Suddenly LIV’s chief executive, Scott O’Neil, was forced to take his begging bowl up and down midtown Manhattan, panhandling for change, drawing up entirely conceptual revenue forecasts, pretending for all the world that this was an actual, real-lif

articles.title: Andy Burnham is in danger of over-selling his big Brussels summit. What happens if he under-delivers? | Joël Reland
articles.description: In laying a trap for himself, the PM could derail his longer-term ambition of revisiting Brexit This week’s UK-EU summit may, one day, be seen as the start of the UK’s long march back towards the EU. Andy Burnham’s much-anticipated first meeting with EU chiefs in Brussels on Friday will be used to unveil a suite of detailed agreements to improve trade and economic cooperation, before the Prime Minister kickstarts his longer term “national conversation” about a much closer form of political and economic relationship with the EU. This, as Burnham signalled in a speech on Monday night , could well culminate in Labour’s next election manifesto abandoning the party’s famous red lines, and proposing an application for EU membership. For pro-Europeans, this must read like a fever dream. Just four months ago, when Burnham took office, such a bold offer on Europe from the Labour party seemed implausible. But while Burnham has certainly reinvigorated the Brexit debate, he will have to move carefully to avoid storing up trouble for himself down the road. There is a risk that Burnham will come to be seen as someone who over-promises and under-delivers on Europe – and, in doing so, halts the gr

articles.title: Gonzalo García: ‘I love Craven Cottage – the fans can reach out and touch you’
articles.description: Spain Under-21 striker admits the pace of the Premier League has surprised him but says he must stay calm over goal drought at Fulham The first thing Rita Hayworth’s great nephew says when he walks in is: “Sorry I’m late.” Gonzalo García is not late, but it’s very like him: he is impeccably polite, accommodating, and there’s an almost gentle quality to him, a calm that’s not common but can help, especially in moments when the pressure builds. There’s a reason one of the coaches standing in the rain by the pitch where Spain’s under-21s have just finished training says everyone here loves García. The Fulham striker shakes hands, introduces himself and ducks into the dressing room to change; then a few minutes later he’s back, apologising for a wait that wasn’t one. Time to talk, so let’s start with tinseltown, the family tale. García laughs. His great-aunt, born Margarita Carmen Cansino, was among the biggest stars in Hollywood, although he’s not sure he’s seen any of her films. His grandfather was a surgeon and others in the family followed. His uncles played rugby for Spain, but that wasn’t his thing. As for him, he enrolled in a degree in business management and analytics, and rec

articles.title: From training clips to thirst traps: why athletes are turning to OnlyFans
articles.description: A professional sports career does not guarantee wealth. And a growing number of athletes are turning to alternative streams of income “I’m sick and tired of it.” Bart Swings tossed his jacket behind him. It was August 2025, the Winter Olympics were less than six months away, and the Belgian Olympic champion’s injured knee was not getting better. The clip, profanity and all, later ran on the Belgian evening news along with the weather and the football. But the injury update didn’t come from an interview – it was broadcast on the speed skater’s OnlyFans channel. The subscription site, best known for porn dudes, cam girls and dubiously horny couples, has quietly assembled one of the stranger rosters in professional sport. The list, about 285 athletes deep, includes Olympic speed skaters and rowers, tennis players, surfers and golfers. And, despite its racy reputation, many of the athletes on OnlyFans are not putting out adult content. Continue reading...

articles.title: England’s ‘fresh’ rookies roll on to Australia T20s as Test stars depart early
articles.description: Root, Duckett, Archer, Atkinson and Baker head home McCullum: ‘Brook has an unbelievable tactical brain’ Fresh from turning over Australia in the 50-over leg of this tour, England’s attention now turns to the Twenty20s that start on Saturday. Five players jet home for a swift breather before the Tests in South Africa, with fresh-faced rookies coming in. Joe Root, Ben Duckett, Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson and Sonny Baker were the men heading for the departure lounge, while captain Harry Brook and wicketkeeper Jordan Cox will leave after the fourth of the five T20Is on 29 November. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Closing the door halts growth’: Liv Apps on PWR’s international appeal – and pruning the Red Roses
articles.description: Saracens and Canada scrum-half believes having fewer overseas players in England’s top tier would be a backwards step both for her and the wider game Liv Apps understands only too well the benefits of playing in Premiership Women’s Rugby (PWR), so when challenging the views of the Red Roses’ head coach, John Mitchell, it comes from the heart. According to the Saracens and Canada scrum-half, limiting the international talent pool in England’s elite division would halt the growth of the game, or even dilute the PWR’s potency. “For us Canadians, it is amazing to have the PWR because we don’t have a league at home. But then also what the Canadians and the other internationals bring to the England players, we all make each other better.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Danny Kelly loved football and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living talking about it | Max Rushden
articles.description: The journalist and broadcaster who died last week aged 69 knew the enduring power of radio, even as the landscape changed so quickly It’s injury time at the Emirates on the 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Spurs. Tom Huddlestone cushions a ball to Luka Modric, whose strike takes a deflection. It loops over Manuel Almunia and on to the post into the path of Aaron Lennon, who prods it home and starts skipping towards the Spurs fans before diving on to the ground and being enveloped by Modric, Benoît Assou-Ekotto, Darren Bent and a couple of pitch-invading fans. Pandemonium, for once, seems the apt way to describe it. But the real entertainment is happening in a radio studio at 18 Hatfields, London SE1; the old home of TalkSport. As the goal goes in, a guttural voice makes an indecipherable but very loud noise. It’s hard to transcribe – perhaps “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH”, or maybe “OOEEERRAAGGH”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Race for the Fifa presidency: lineup revealed to challenge Gianni Infantino
articles.description: Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima are both standing But Ramon Vega fails to get the necessary backing Fifa has confirmed that Gianni Infantino will face challenges from Philippe Diallo of France and Japan’s Kozo Tashima in March’s presidential election. The president of the French Football Federation and honorary president of the Japan Football Association submitted nomination letters with endorsements from five member associations by Wednesday night’s midnight CET deadline. The former Switzerland and Tottenham defender Ramon Vega has not met that threshold, despite repeatedly saying he would stand. Continue reading...

articles.title: World marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir banned for three years over doping
articles.description: Three leading Kenyan distance runners all sanctioned Jepchirchir also won the Olympic gold medal in Tokyo The reigning world marathon champion, Peres Jepchirchir, has been hit with a three-year ban for EPO on a dismal day for Kenyan distance running, with two other leading distance athletes from the country also being punished for doping. The 33-year-old Jepchirchir, who won Olympic and world gold in Tokyo in 2021 and 2025 respectively, had her ban reduced by a year after she decided not to challenge the results of a blood test taken before winning the Sydney marathon in August . Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I see comments every day’: Sonay Kartal’s fightback against injury and online abuse
articles.description: British tennis star has bounced back after six months out but wants more to be done about vitriol aimed at players Sonay Kartal believes the vitriolic abuse and threats that she and her fellow players receive after every match have become an unavoidable part of her job. “Unfortunately, it’s something that comes with the sport,” the British No 2 says. “I don’t really have a choice to not deal with it. Obviously, it’s not a good thing to have and as a player, win or lose, you’re seeing those things. Continue reading...

articles.title: Weight-loss drugs used in nearly one in 10 homes in Great Britain, study finds
articles.description: About 2.6m adults are taking the drugs, fuelled by the regulator’s approval of the pill versions and a rise in male users At least one person is taking weight-loss drugs in 8.5% of households in Great Britain, according to research, meaning there are more homes with GLP-1 users than those containing vegetarians and pescatarians combined. About 2.6 million adults were using weight-loss medication in August, a rise of about 700,000 people since February, according to a survey by Worldpanel by Numerator . Continue reading...

articles.title: Meet Phil, the bar-tailed godwit tracked on a 6,800-mile round trip to Siberia
articles.description: Scientists use lightweight tracker to map wading bird’s extraordinary migration from Norfolk to the Arctic and back A bar-tailed godwit called Phil has completed a 6,800-mile journey from Norfolk to Siberia and back again, in the first mapping of the endurance feats of this long-distance migrant. A wading bird not much larger than a pigeon, the bar-tailed godwit is known for making the longest recorded non-stop migratory flight of any bird, with populations that visit Britain spending summers breeding in the Arctic Circle before retreating to the unfrozen wetlands of Britain in winter. Continue reading...

articles.title: Car use in London forecast to rise by 10% in next decade
articles.description: Modelling in draft of 10-year London plan threatens Sadiq Khan’s promises on improving air quality Car use in London will rise by 10% over the next decade with cycling and walking falling as a proportion of trips, according to an official forecast by the city’s mayoralty, putting into doubt Sadiq Khan’s promises on air quality and the environment. Based on projections in the draft version of the latest 10-year London plan , drawn up by the mayor’s office and Transport for London (TfL), road congestion from a growing population would slow buses down, while packed tube services might require stations to close regularly to ease numbers. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tulip Siddiq says she is considering legal action against former Bangladesh leader
articles.description: Former minister, who was sentenced to prison in Bangladesh in her absence, says she was victim of ‘malicious prosecution’ The former minister Tulip Siddiq has said she is considering taking legal action against the former interim leader of Bangladesh over corruption allegations made by his administration led her to resign from the UK government last year. The MP for Hampstead and Highgate, whose aunt Sheikh Hasina was put on trial in absentia over crimes against humanity during her 15 years as prime minister of Bangladesh, was accused of benefiting from the former regime by the authorities in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka. Continue reading...

articles.title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
articles.description: Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report. In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund ( UNFPA ) published on Thursday. Continue reading...

articles.title: Violent protests and killings in Bangladesh ahead of exiled Sheikh Hasina’s planned return
articles.description: Awami League party called for ⁠nationwide protest on Thursday after the government rejected Hasina’s request for passport Parts of Bangladesh were shut down Thursday as protests by supporters of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina sparked clashes, bomb blasts and arson attacks, with the ancestral home ⁠of former leader Muhammad Yunus set ablaze in the violence. Hasina’s Awami League party had called for a ​week-long programme of protests and rallies to mobilise support ‌for Hasina’s planned return in December , culminating in a ‌nationwide lockdown on Thursday. Continue reading...

articles.title: EDF snaps up 1.3m more customers after Utilita takeover
articles.description: Great Britain’s fourth-largest energy supplier brings account base up to 6m after purchase of pay-as-you-go supplier EDF Energy will grow its share of the UK’s household energy market to more than 6m customer accounts after snapping up the pay-as-you-go supplier Utilita. Great Britain’s fourth-largest energy supplier expects to complete the takeover early next year, adding 1.3m accounts to its customer base and taking on Utilita’s 1,500 staff. The price of the deal was undisclosed. Continue reading...

articles.title: How years of research built Grand Theft Auto VI’s obsessively detailed world
articles.description: The developers behind its virtual Florida share how they built their most ambitious world so far • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In 2015, a group of Grand Theft Auto developers from Rockstar North took their first trips to Miami to do field research for the next game in the phenomenally popular crime series. “Before you’re doing hyper-organised research trips, you’re immersing yourself in the place and its history, the vibe of it,” Rob Nelson, one of the lead developers on GTA VI, tells me. “[You see] the physical places you want to move characters through, the experiences you want them to have, and the juxtaposition between the extremes of society that are in Miami.” I wondered: did people ever recognise them on any of their research trips? Did locals know what they were doing? This is the biggest game in the world, after all; I imagine it would be difficult to go entirely undercover. “We’re always semi-undercover,” he says. “But if you have a bunch of dorks going through a terrifying neighbourhood, you do stick out a bit.” Continue reading...
